articles.title: Reddit (and everyone else) faces a bleak internet without Google traffic
articles.summary: Silicon Valley's embrace of AI may come at the cost of huge swaths of the web — and the companies that rely on Google traffic to operate.
articles.body:
Google zero, eventually, comes for us all .

That's the belief, and fear, that meaningful traffic from Google trends toward zero because of changes to its search engine practices and, more recently, its shift toward AI — answering people's search questions not with links to places like websites, but with AI summaries and chatbot dialogue.

Reddit's ( RDDT ) latest earnings report was a reckoning of Google's AI-led changes . And it underscored how Silicon Valley's full embrace of AI may come at the cost of huge swaths of the web — and the companies that rely on Google traffic to operate.

"People still want Reddit. It is just Google is not sending them to Reddit the way they used to," Steve Huffman, Reddit's co-founder and CEO, said on an earnings call earlier this week.

The company reported that search referral traffic was down meaningfully in the past quarter. Google's shift to AI mode and AI overviews has halted traffic that once flowed to the social forum.

"Google is crawling us as hard as ever, so the demand hasn't changed from their point of view either," Huffman said. "The reality is the AI Mode does not drive traffic. Not for us, and not to anybody as far as I know."

The shift toward a more AI-inflicted internet isn't just hurting Reddit. It's hurting Google too , at least in the short term. Its parent company, Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), shed almost $500 billion (or about two Netflixes) in market value after reporting a slowdown in its core search advertising business, in part due to the lower profitability of AI ads.

A critical view of the whole situation is that Google is smothering online publishers and sabotaging its own legacy business in its rush toward AI dominance.

But Reddit took a stance on the call that could be described as corporate Zen: "For AI Overviews and traffic, look, we don't control Google. We only control Reddit."

The company said it's not counting on that once-sweet Google traffic returning and plans to require all users to create Reddit accounts and sign in to access the site.

Other online publishers are looking to subscriptions to create direct relationships with audiences and are partnering with AI companies to ride the next wave of LLM-based media and product distribution.

Google, for its part, continues to argue the case (although not persuasively, given the stock plunge) that its AI efforts will prevail, even if it's still trying to figure out the problem of how to make more money with it.

Google executives no doubt disagree with the market sell-off, which has dragged the company's price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio back to levels not seen since 2012. Management knew this transition was coming. Their contention is that the success of AI tools will generate a new and different business model, and that it will be more profitable than the search-and-click paradigm the rest of the web relied on.

The bull case is that Google has good reasons to choose this bumpy path. But that also happens to be a bear case for almost everyone else.

articles.title: Centre scraps Rs 2.5/litre petrol export duty, hikes diesel levy to Rs 11.5
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Centre has scrapped the Rs 2.5 per litre special additional excise duty (SAED) on petrol exports while raising the levy on high-speed
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Centre has scrapped the Rs 2.5 per litre special additional excise duty (SAED) on petrol exports while raising the levy on high-speed diesel from Rs 8.5 to Rs 11.5 per litre and on aviation turbine fuel (ATF) from Rs 10.5 to Rs 11 per litre, according to notifications issued by the Ministry of Finance on Saturday.The revised rates have been notified by the Department of Revenue through separate excise notifications. While the changes to petrol and diesel duties have been covered under the relevant excise notification, Notification No. 56/2026-Central Excise specifically provides for the increase in the levy on ATF exports.All the revised rates took effect on October 31, the date of their publication in the official Gazette.The export duties on petrol, diesel and ATF were first introduced on March 27, 2026, against the backdrop of the West Asia crisis. The Centre had stated that the move was aimed at discouraging exports to ensure that petroleum products remained available in the domestic market.The introduction of the levies came amid rising international energy prices and uncertainty over supplies, which had raised concerns about the availability of petroleum products within the country.Since then, the government has been revising the duties every fortnight. The exercise takes into account the average international prices of crude oil, petrol, diesel and ATF during the period following the previous review.The rates have seen multiple changes since the initial announcement, reflecting movements in international prices. Before the latest revision, the duties stood at Rs 2.5 per litre on petrol, Rs 8.5 per litre on high-speed diesel and Rs 10.5 per litre on ATF, following the October 16 review.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Binance will absorb the impact, not users’: Crypto exchange sets aside $6.34 billion to cover hack losses
articles.summary: After facing a major crypto theft, Binance has assured users that they won’t lose money over the breach.
articles.body: After facing a major crypto theft, Binance has assured users that they won’t lose money over the breach.The exchange is covering the $6.3 billion loss from its own funds, setting aside more than $6.34 billion to make up for the stolen assets. It has already replaced around 80 per cent of the stolen tokens and is working to restore withdrawal services in phases.So far, Binance has bought back $5 billion worth of the stolen cryptocurrencies, including USDC, USDT, Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and BNB. It is now working on getting the remaining tokens back through market and OTC purchases."This means that we have already covered approximately 80% of the impacted amount. We are actively buying the remaining relevant token assets through market and OTC channels," Binance said.In its second update on the recovery process, the company said the compensation would be funded through its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and corporate treasury."We want to be clear about our commitment: Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the exchange said in the statement.$3 billion in stolen assets frozenThe breach took place at around 20:05 UTC on October 29, when Binance's hot wallets were compromised, leading to unauthorised withdrawals of approximately $6.3 billion worth of digital assets.Alongside replacing the stolen assets, the exchange said it had managed to freeze approximately $3 billion worth of the stolen funds across blockchain networks. The effort involved coordination with law enforcement agencies, blockchain intelligence firms, asset issuers and industry partners.Binance is targeting the phased restoration of withdrawal services within approximately 34 hours, although the timeline remains subject to the completion of security checks. Deposits and other platform services unaffected by the breach continue to remain operational.The exchange also plans to release an updated Proof of Reserves report by Monday, November 2, enabling users to check the digital assets backing their account balances.Binance finds additional points of breach in investigationBinance's investigation into the incident has also uncovered more details about how the security breach may have occurred. While the initial assessment pointed towards a compromised laptop, subsequent findings indicated that there were additional points of intrusion."Our initial investigation suggested that the incident may involve a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," it said.The company said it had found no evidence of wallet private keys being leaked. Further technical findings are expected within approximately 48 hours, subject to verification.North Korean hacking group linked to $6.3 billion theftSeparately, blockchain investigation firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the $6.3 billion theft to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor, Reuters reported.Cybersecurity experts cited by Reuters said money generated through North Korean cryptocurrency thefts has helped finance the country's weapons programmes. However, Binance has not publicly identified the perpetrators and maintained that its investigation is ongoing.The exchange said it would release a detailed technical report explaining how the breach took place, along with the additional security measures it plans to introduce to prevent similar incidents.You use AI every day. articles.title: How to grow a nest egg while protecting it from inflation and market drops
articles.summary: There is nothing more agitating for everyday investors than markets falling out of bed and rising inflation eating away at their wallets.
articles.body: There is nothing more agitating for everyday investors than markets falling out of bed and rising inflation eating away at their wallets. Certified financial planner Douglas Boneparth offers his best advice for how to quell that agitation with a smart, long-term investment strategy A reader from Maryland asks: How do I grow the money I have and hedge against inflation and the next market correction? DOUG: Two things make investors nervous about the future: Inflation eroding their purchasing power, and a market correction suddenly shrinking their portfolio. They feel like different threats, but a well-constructed investment strategy can address both at the same time. Let’s start with inflation. The best long-term hedge against inflation historically has been owning assets that grow faster than prices do. That generally means staying invested in stocks because they have outpaced inflation over long periods more consistently than almost anything else. Beyond that, assets like real estate and commodities can provide additional insulation, though they have their own risks and complexities. Now, about market corrections. Corrections are normal. They happen regularly, they feel terrible every time, and they have historically been followed by recoveries. The best hedge against them isn’t trying to time your way out of the market. That’s a game almost no one wins. Rather, it’s having a diversified portfolio that matches your time horizon and risk tolerance, so when the market drops, you’re not forced to sell at the wrong time. Both concerns point to the same solution. A diversified, long-term investment strategy that you don’t abandon when things get uncomfortable. The investors who get hurt most in corrections are the ones who panic. The ones who stay the course, and better yet, keep investing through the dip, tend to come out ahead. If you don’t already work with a financial advisor, this is a good time to consider it. Creating a strategy that balances growth and protection depends on your timeline, your income, and how you handle stress when the market is down 20% or more. Those are conversations worth having with someone who can help you build a plan and stick to it. Tip of the week: Know what your enough is When it comes to how much money you should save and how you should invest, the best answers are based on your needs, preferences, temperament and timeline. Sure, it’s good advice for most people to save at least enough in a 401(k) to get their full company match and ideally more than that. But how big your own nest egg should be depends on personal factors, like when you retire, whether you’ll have a pension and how much you plan to spend. So forget aiming for some nebulous “best.” Instead consider what your own “enough” is and aim for that. And bonus: If you already find life complex enough, you don’t have to soak yourself in the intricacies of the market and multiple investing strategies to reach your goal. In fact, you may get where you need to go using a simpler approach and sticking with a few low-cost index funds that track market performance over time.

articles.title: Math teacher gets a plan to keep his debt from derailing his retirement
articles.summary: A financial plan by certified financial planner showed the 57-year-old that he could retire comfortably at his desired age of 75
articles.body: In CNN’s first update on math teacher and tennis coach Jeff Kizer, we described him as “chill” when it came to money and noted he didn’t see it as a source for happiness. But being chill didn’t mean Jeff hasn’t been worried about his financial prospects. A financial plan by certified financial planner Craig Toberman showed Jeff, 57, that he could retire comfortably at his desired age of 75 despite having less than $200,000 in his nest egg today, a heavy debt load and a 14-year-old daughter likely to go to college in a few years. Jeff expressed surprise and relief that things could work out for him financially so long as he stayed disciplined and methodical about paying down his debts and working consistently over the next 18 years. “I was ecstatic about where I am going to end up,” he said. Top priority now? Ease up on savings to clear debts Craig’s biggest recommendation is for Jeff to actually save less for retirement and instead redirect money to pay off two of his three loans in the next few years. At this writing, Jeff had nearly $165,000 saved for retirement, including a $10,000 IRA. And he had been socking away 17% of his $73,000 teacher’s salary and 10% of his $40,000 tennis salary plus employer matches. Craig recommends Jeff lower his 17% contribution rate to 10% at his school. That’s still enough to get his employer’s full matching contribution. And combined with the money he is contributing to the 401(k) at his tennis job, he will still be saving more than 14% of his combined $113,000 pre-tax income for retirement. Craig calculates that a 7% drop in Jeff’s contributions at school will free up $4,200 a year after tax – or $350 per month. Craig wants Jeff to add that $350 to his current monthly payments on his $33,000 personal loan that has a 10.23% interest rate. That way, he’ll be paying a total of $1,216 each month. And in doing so, the loan will be paid off in two years instead of three, Craig said. When it is, he then suggests Jeff redirect the $1,216 to pay down his roughly $50,000 student loan that has a 5.36% interest rate. That will boost his total monthly payment on that loan to $1,401. If he does that, the student loan should be paid off by the time Jeff’s daughter is ready to go to college in 2031, Craig said. At that point, he can repurpose the $1,401 a month to help pay her college costs. And by the time she’s a sophomore in 2032, Craig noted, Jeff will have yet more money to put toward college: His $75,000 truck loan, on which he’s paying $1,092 a month, will be paid off. That will then give him $2,493 a month ($1,401 + $1,092) to further help with his daughter’s tuition. (Side note: Craig said Jeff promised he will drive that truck for many years and noted if anything goes awry with Jeff’s finances, he should sell it in addition to cutting back on other spending.) Wait on Social Security Another key suggestion for Jeff is to wait until 70 to claim Social Security, at which point his expected benefit will be $48,624 a year. “He should bank that money while he continues to work until 75,” Craig suggested. If he does that and continues contributing to his 401(k)s until age 75, Jeff could have over $1 million in his mid-70s, “which should be sufficient with Social Security to have a most likely stress-free retirement,” Craig said. That assumes an average annual return of 6.34% in his portfolio until his retirement year and then 5.48% thereafter. For all that to happen, though, Jeff needs to keep working, live within his means and not tap his nest egg before he retires. Craig’s advice: “Stay healthy, stay happy and take care of yourself. Like your job. Don’t blow it. Don’t tell off your bosses.” If Jeff does all these things, Craig said, “He has a sufficient probability of never having to worry about money.” What’s next: We’ll follow up again with Jeff in a few weeks. But next week we’ll catch up with Abbey Graf, who will learn whether she has a solid chance at early retirement.

articles.title: Swipe, shop, repeat: Online buyers splash out 7.5% more than offline shoppers
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Do you feel your bills have gone up since you started using e-commerce apps? Don’t worry, you are not alone!
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Do you feel your bills have gone up since you started using e-commerce apps? Don’t worry, you are not alone!A few taps on your phone could mean a bigger shopping bill. Indian households that use online shopping and payment platforms spend 7.5 per cent more every month than those that do not. The gap is even wider when it comes to services and durable goods. However, the shift to online shopping is far from uniform, with digital adoption still closely linked to household income, according to a report by SBI Research.The report found that households using digital platforms spend 23.4 per cent more on services and 24.5 per cent more on durable goods than those that do not.However, not all households have made the move from traditional shopping to online purchases.Digital shopping still has a long way to goLess than half of Indian households have embraced online purchases and payments. According to the report, 45.6 per cent of households used online purchase or payment facilities for at least one consumption item, while 54.4 per cent reported no such usage.The income divide is particularly wide. Among households in the bottom 20 per cent consumption quintile, only 25.3 per cent used online platforms. The share rose to 69.5 per cent among the top 20 per cent, leaving a gap of 44.3 percentage points.The findings are based on a fixed-effects log-linear model that accounts for household characteristics and state-district factors.Groceries make the online basketWhen it comes to digital purchases, consumables and services account for the largest share at 39.68 per cent, followed by durable goods at 23.3 per cent. Food items, meanwhile, make up just 7.10 per cent of online purchases.Within the food category, groceries lead digital adoption at 4.29 per cent. The numbers drop for everyday fresh produce, with online purchases accounting for 1.32 per cent for vegetables and 1 per cent for fresh fruits. Dry fruits account for 0.62 per cent, while eggs, fish and meat make up just 0.59 per cent.SBI Research attributed the limited adoption of online platforms for perishable food items to households' continued preference for traditional retail channels.Many consumers still prefer visiting markets for their daily food purchases.Clothing takes the lead among online durable purchasesNot all durable goods are equally popular online.Clothing recorded the highest digital adoption at 19.97 per cent, followed by footwear at 12.05 per cent. Online purchases of furniture, medical equipment and recreational goods, however, remained limited.At the same time, services accounted for the largest share of online purchases within the consumables and services category at 37.93 per cent. Fuel and light followed at 15.96 per cent.SBI Research said digital adoption was associated with higher consumption intensity and more diversified household spending. However, the substantial difference in adoption across income groups shows that the shift towards online shopping is yet to reach all sections of the country equally.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fed Chairman Warsh's latest press conference leaves Wall Street guessing — again
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh held his fourth press conference this week and once again left Wall Street scrambling to guess his next move.
articles.body:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh held his fourth press conference this week, and when it came to defining the economy, inflation, and the path for rate hikes, he once again left Wall Street scrambling to guess his next move.

Michael Feroli, chief US economist for JPMorgan, said the press conference "left something to be desired," most notably, "a simple explanation for why the committee didn't tighten."

The performance harkened back to Warsh's July press conference when the chair left markets with a lack of clarity about the Fed's willingness to raise rates. Warsh repeatedly pointed to bond yields shooting higher, suggesting it was a good thing and implying that the Fed welcomes higher yields to tighten policy through markets. His stance initially triggered higher long-term bond yields, causing confusion and damaging market confidence in the Fed's strategy.

Warsh responded in a highly anticipated speech at the Fed's annual symposium in August, giving Wall Street a measure of clarity on how the central bank would respond to rising prices.

But some analysts saw his press conference this week as a step backward.

When pressed by reporters on why the central bank refrained from raising rates , Warsh avoided direct economic measures. Instead, Feroli said Warsh veered into a winding, abstract maze of rhetoric, invoking phrases like "new monetary medicine," "interrogating reality," and "looking out the window."

Feroli pointed to New York Fed president John Williams and Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, who both offered rationales ahead of the meeting for accumulating more data before raising rates further.

"One can debate the merits of the arguments for a pause laid out by Williams and others, but at least they were couched in a discussion of the economic data," Feroli said. "Without a clear answer, it is understandable that the market has become a little less convinced there is a plan to tighten in December."

The Fed's policy statement added a line echoing Jefferson and Williams, saying "the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."

Greg Daco, chief economist for EY, took the added sentence to mean that this week's decision was a "hawkish hold," but he said Warsh still "fell short" by failing to provide a coherent argument for not raising rates.

"Saying that the Fed is not committed to a data point or a date does little to assuage concerns about inflationary pressures," Daco said. "There is indeed a contradiction in talking tough on price stability after a six-year-long overshoot and refusing to take ownership by repeatedly saying the Fed is 'interrogating reality' by 'looking out the window' to gauge true economic conditions."
